sentences.text: He is sentenced to suffer imprisonment for 10 (ten) years and to pay fine of Rs.10,000/- and in default to suffer RI for 3 (three) months for the offence punishable under Section 6 of the POCSO Act ; and to suffer imprisonment for 6 (six) months and to pay fine of Rs.1,000/- and in default to suffer RI for one month for the offence punishable under Section 323 of the IPC.
No separate sentence is awarded for the offence punishable under Section 376(2)(n) of the IPC.

2. BACKGROUND FACTS :-
PW1 is the informant and the father of the victim girl.
The victim (PW2), on the date of the alleged incident, was 15 years of age.
The case of the prosecution, which can be gathered from the report and the other materials, is that on 15.03.2019 at about 7.00 p.m., the informant found that the victim was missing from the house.
He took search of the victim, however, she could not be traced out.

The informant, therefore,
went to Police Station, Imamwada, Nagpur and lodged a missing report on the same day.
The victim girl was traced out 3 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt by Imamwada police station on 24.03.2019 at Manmad.
The police recorded her statement.
It is further the case of the prosecution that the victim narrated the alleged incident to the police.
It is stated that on 15.03.2019 at about 1.30 pm, she left the house without intimating her family members.
She went to Manmad by train to meet her brother Monu.
She reached Manmad railway station at around 00.30 hours on 16.03.2019.
She got down at Manmad railway station.
It is stated that at that time one boy came to her and started making inquiry with her.
The boy, on an inquiry made by the victim, disclosed his name as Avinash i.e. appellant.
The victim disclosed to said Avinash i.e. appellant, the purpose of her visit to Manmad.
The appellant asked the victim to stay with him at his house in the night.

The victim, believing the appellant,
accompanied him to his house.
The appellant took her to a place like hostel.
At the said hostel like place, they took dinner together.
After dinner, the appellant demanded sexual favour from the victim.
The appellant, against the consent of the victim, committed rape on her.
The appellant, on the next day, before proceeding to his workplace, warned the victim not to leave the place.

However,
the victim went to meet her brother Monu.
The victim disclosed to the appellant that she had gone to meet Monu.
The 4 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt appellant got angry and beat her.
It is stated that the appellant again established physical relations with the victim by force.
The victim stayed with the appellant for 2 to 3 days.
The victim made a phone call to her father from the mobile phone of the appellant and informed that she was at Manmad.
The victim was, thereafter, brought to Nagpur by police.
Her statement was recorded.

On the basis of the further information provided by the victim,
the investigation in the crime, bearing Crime No. 71/2019, which was already registered at Imamwada police station, Nagpur, was carried out by PW7.
The investigation led to the filing of charge-sheet against the appellant.
3. Learned Additional Sessions Judge framed the charge (Exh. 3) against the appellant.
The appellant pleaded not guilty.
His defence is of false implication in the crime.

sentences.text: The learned Sessions Judge, on consideration of the evidence, held the appellant guilty and sentenced him as above.
The appellant, being aggrieved by the said judgment and order, has come before this Court in appeal.
5 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt 4.

I have heard Mr. Sunil Kulkarni, learned advocate holding for Mrs. Sunita Kulkarni, learned advocate for the appellant, Mr. Amit R. Chutke, learned Additional Public Prosecutor for respondent no.1/State and Ms. Radha Mishra, learned advocate appointed to represent respondent no.2/victim.
Perused the record and proceedings.

5. As far as the age of the victim is concerned, perusal of the evidence on record shows that the same is sufficient to prove that the victim, on the date of the incident, was 14 years, 6 months and 9 days old.
The victim (PW2), in her evidence, has stated that her birth date is 06.10.2004.

PW1 informant,
who is the father of the victim, has also stated that the victim was born on 06.10.2004.
The Investigating Officer had collected the documentary evidence with regard to the birth date of the victim.
The birth certificate of the victim obtained from the Heath Department of the Nagpur Municipal Corporation, is at Exh.39.

As per Exh.40, the Government Medical College and Hospital,
Nagpur, had intimated the Health Department of the Municipal Corporation, Nagpur, about the birth of the victim.

Perusal of their cross- examination would show that neither the birth date nor the documents with regard to the birth date of the victim,
have been challenged.

sentences.text: 3 7 . The next important question that has to be addressed is, whether the alleged incident, as narrated by the victim (PW2), has occurred and the appellant was involved in the said incident ?

Learned advocate appearing for the appellant submitted that the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the prosecution would show that prior to the date of the alleged incident, the appellant was not known to the victim.
The test identification parade of the appellant during the course of investigation was not conducted.
It is further submitted that the prosecution has failed to adduce sufficient evidence to establish the involvement of the appellant in the crime.
It is submitted that neither the informant nor the police have stated as to how and when they came to know about the involvement of the appellant.
Learned advocate 8 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt further submitted that the evidence of the victim girl is not sufficient to prove the involvement of the appellant in this crime.
Her evidence is doubtful.
Her conduct is inconsistent and unnatural.

A person by name Manubhau,
to whom the victim has been treating as her brother, has not been examined.
The victim has stated that on the next day of the alleged incident, she met Manubhau.
It is pointed out that she did not narrate this incident to Manubhau.
It is submitted that this is a doubtful circumstance.

Learned advocate took me through the history of assault narrated by the victim to the Medical Officer at the time of her examination and pointed out that she did not mention the name of the appellant.

In fact,
before the Doctor, she had stated that the intercourse was committed with her by her boyfriend and one more person.
It is submitted that it is not the case of the prosecution that the appellant was the boyfriend of the victim.

Learned advocate submitted that in her statement recorded by the learned Judicial Magistrate, First Class, Nagpur, she had stated that 4 to 5 boys chased her at the railway station and thereafter she went to one room with the appellant.
Learned advocate submitted that the evidence of the victim is not sufficient to establish the involvement of the appellant in this crime.

The victim has already stated that there were other boys involved in the 9 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt alleged incident and therefore, the medical evidence by itself would not be sufficient to establish the complicity of the appellant in this crime.
8.
Learned APP submitted that the informant (PW1) and the victim (PW2) had no reason to falsely implicate the appellant.
The appellant, on an inquiry with the victim, told his name as Avinash to her and therefore, the victim rightly stated the name of the appellant to her father as well as to the police.
It is submitted that the appellant taking advantage of the situation, forcibly committed penetrative sexual assault on the victim.
The victim, on the date of the crime, was 15 years of age.
It is submitted that the defence of consent is not available to the appellant.
In short, learned APP submitted that a well reasoned judgment and order passed by the learned Sessions Judge does not warrant interference.
9. It is to be noted at the outset that the medical evidence is sufficient to prove that the victim girl was subjected to sexual intercourse.

PW3 Dr. Ashwinkumar Sontakke, on examination of the victim,
noticed multiple old hymen tears at 3, 6 and 12 O'clock position.
PW3 also noticed other injuries on the body of the victim.
10 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt PW3 opined that sexual intercourse could not be ruled out.
The victim was further examined by PW4 Dr. Roshan Ingle.
He found multiple injuries on the person of the victim.
It is to be noted that in the medical certificate (Exh.20), issued by PW3, and the medical certificate (Exh.22), issued by PW4, the age of the injuries has not been mentioned.

Be that as it Avinash Vijay Kharat vs State Of Mah. Thr. Pso Ps Imamwada Nagpur ... on 9 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/185701459/
4 may, the fact remains that the presence of the injuries on the private part of the victim proves that she was subjected to sexual intercourse.

sentences.text: 10. The important question which needs to be addressed in this case is whether the appellant had committed sexual intercourse with the victim or not ?

On minute perusal and scrutiny of the evidence of the victim (PW2) and the informant (PW1), I am satisfied that this evidence owefully falls short to establish the complicity of the appellant in this crime.
Admittedly, the appellant was not known to the victim prior to the alleged incident.
During the investigation, the test identification parade of the appellant was not conducted.
Perusal of the evidence of the victim would show that on the date of her evidence, the appellant was produced via video conferencing.
The victim identified the appellant when he was produced through video conferencing.
11 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt
There is no explanation for not conducting the test identification parade at the stage of the investigation.
Perusal of the evidence of the informant and the Investigating Officer would show that they have proceeded on the assumption that the victim was knowing the appellant prior to this incident.
The person by name Manubhau has not been examined.
It is the case of the prosecution that the victim had gone to Manmad by train to meet Manubhau.
It has come on record that the victim was treating Manubhau as her brother.
She has also stated in her evidence that on the next day of the incident, she had met Manubhau and came back to the place of the incident.
The appellant came to know about it and he beat her.
She has stated that she stayed with the appellant for 3 to 4 days.
It is to be noted that if the alleged incident had occurred in the night, then on the next day when the victim met her brother Manubhau, she would have narrated the incident to him.
In my view, this is a very doubtful circumstance in this case.
11. The informant (PW1) i.e. father, while lodging the report (Exh.8), did not state that the appellant was known to him, or to the victim, prior to the alleged incident.

In his evidence, the father has stated that after two days of lodging missing report of the victim, he 12 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt received a phone call from the mobile phone of the appellant and his daughter (victim) talked to him.
In his substantive evidence, the informant is silent about the name of the appellant.
It is also not his case that the victim told him about the alleged incident occurred with her.
If the appellant had committed forcible sexual intercourse with the victim, then he would not have allowed the victim girl to use his mobile phone for calling her father.

If the victim had used the mobile phone of the appellant, as stated by the informant and the victim, then she, at that time, would have informed her father about the alleged incident and involvement of the appellant.
It is not the case of the informant (PW1) that in the presence of the appellant, she made a phone call to him and informed him about occurrence of the alleged incident.
In my view, this is also an important fact, which needs to be considered while appreciating the evidence.

In his evidence, the informant (PW1) has not stated that the victim, after coming to Nagpur, told the name of the appellant as Avinash and the sexual intercourse was committed with her by said Avinash.
12. The evidence of the victim girl (PW2) would show that she was in habit of leaving the house without informing her family 13 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt members.
In her cross-examination, she has stated that prior to March- 2019, she had left the house once without intimating her parents.
At that time, she had gone Manmad.
She has stated that in March-2019, she had travelled by train without Avinash Vijay Kharat vs State Of Mah. Thr. Pso Ps Imamwada Nagpur ...

5 ticket.
She reached Manmad in the night at about 00.30 hours.
She was sitting at the railway station.
She has stated that at that time, one person came and made an inquiry with her.
The said person told his name as Avinash.
Avinash took her to a hostel by auto-rikshaw.
They had meals and thereafter, the appellant committed intercourse with her.
She has stated that on the next day, she went to meet Manubhau without intimating the appellant.

It is to be noted that if the appellant was involved in such a serious crime and the sexual intercourse was committed against her consent, then she would have informed about the same to her brother Manubhau.

The victim, in such a situation,
would not have returned to the appellant.
In her substantive evidence, the victim has stated that she had gone to Manmad to meet Manubhau.
This shows that there was bonding between the victim and Manubhau.
She had faith and confidence in Manubhau.
If the appellant had committed forcible sexual intercourse with her, then after meeting Manubhau, she would not have gone back to the appellant.
In my view, this part of the alleged incident appears 14 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt doubtful.
The conduct of the victim appears to be inconsistent and unnatural.
The victim has stated that for the next three days, she stayed with the appellant.
The victim had gone to meet Manubhau.
The victim, in the ordinary course, would not have stayed with the appellant.
This also creates doubt about the involvement of the appellant in the alleged incident.
The appellant was not known to the victim prior to the incident.
It is highly unbelievable that the victim would trust the appellant more than Manubhau.
The conduct of the victim in this context is unbelievable.
Instead of trusting Manubhau, the victim appeared to have trusted the appellant more.
13. In this context, it would be necessary to consider the evidence of the Medical Officer (PW3).
The victim was brought to Imamwada police station.
The Investigating Officer is silent about the source of information, which led them to the victim at Manmad and established the identity of the appellant.
The appellant was arrested on 24.04.2019.
There is no explanation as to why police took one month to arrest the appellant when his involvement was revealed to the police by the victim on 23.03.2019.
The Medical Officer, before conducting the medical examination of the victim, recorded the history of assault 15 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt narrated by her.
Perusal of the history of assault narrated by the victim to the Medical Officer (PW3) would show that she did not state the name of the appellant before the Medical Officer.

She has stated before the Medical Officer that at Manmad,
she met her boyfriend and stayed with her boyfriend for 3 to 4 days.
She has stated that her boyfriend committed sexual intercourse with her for 3 to 4 days.
She has further stated before the Medical Officer that there were two assailants, who had committed intercourse with her.
She has stated that one of them was her boyfriend.
It is to be noted that the appellant was totally stranger to the victim girl when they met for the first time.
Therefore, there was no question of calling the appellant as her boyfriend.
This shows that the person, who was the boyfriend of the victim, was also involved in this offence.
The police have not arrested the boyfriend of the victim.
Similarly, police has failed to establish the identity of said boyfriend.
The victim has stated that the alleged sexual assault was committed on her by two persons.
As per the history of assault narrated by the victim before the Medical Officer, the boyfriend of the victim had committed sexual relations with her.
In view of this, the possibility of causing injury to the hymen due to intercourse with her by her boyfriend, cannot be ruled out.
In my view, this is a very vital 16 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt circumstance to create doubt about the testimony of the victim with regard to the involvement of the appellant in this crime.

6 14.
It is to be noted that during the course of investigation, on the request of the Investigating Officer, the learned Magistrate recorded the statement of the victim under Section 164 of the Cr.P.C.
The statement recorded by the learned Magistrate is part of the record.
The record shows that it has not been exhibited.
It appears that the prosecutor, in-charge of the case, on going through the contents of the statement, did not show the statement to the victim.
Perusal of this statement would show that it is a very vital piece of evidence.
The victim, while recording her statement by the learned Magistrate, stated that due to the cantankerous nature of her parents, she left the house.
She stated that at the railway station, 4 to 5 boys chased her and with those boys, she went to one room.
She has stated that the appellant was one of them.
She stated that the appellant committed sexual intercourse with her.
She stated that from there, she went to her brother Manubhau and stayed with him for one month.
The statement of the victim before the learned Magistrate clearly spells out involvement of 4 to 5 persons in the commission of the crime.
The investigation conducted in the 17 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt crime is conspicuously silent about all these aspects.
The appellant, as can be seen from the record, was not known to the victim prior to the alleged incident.

The appellant,
therefore, could not be the boyfriend of the victim.
The victim did not disclose the name of the boyfriend, who had sexual intercourse with her at that time.
In the facts and circumstances, I am of the opinion that the conviction and sentence on the basis of such tainted evidence cannot be sustained.
Learned Judge ought to have considered all the above stated facts and circumstances.
The doubtful circumstances highlighted hereinabove, would be sufficient to create a serious doubt about the involvement of the appellant in this crime.

15. Though, there is a statutory presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act with respect to the guilt of an accused, this presumption will not operate when the prosecution has failed to prove some foundational facts with respect to the case.
The presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act is not an absolute presumption.
It is a rebuttable presumption.
The presumption gets triggered only when the foundational facts are established by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
The evidence on record must be sufficient to believe 18 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt the case of the prosecution and thereby support the very foundation of the case of the prosecution.
In this case, the very foundation of the case of the prosecution viz-a-viz the charge against the accused has been shaken.
In my view, therefore, the presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act would not get automatically attracted/triggered.
16. There are numerous lacunae in the case.
The prosecution has failed to connect all the dots by leading cogent and concrete evidence.
The evidence of the victim is not sufficient to prove the complicity of the appellant in the commission of the alleged offence.
As such, the appellant deserves benefit of doubt.
The appeal, therefore, deserves to be allowed.

17. The Criminal Appeal is allowed.
(i) The judgment and order of conviction and sentence, passed against the appellant by learned District and Sessions Judge-11, Nagpur, dated 13.01.2022 in Special Child Case No. 160/2019, is quashed and set aside.

10. The important question which needs to be addressed in this case is whether the appellant had committed sexual intercourse with the victim or not ?
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
During the investigation, the test identification parade of the appellant was not conducted.
The victim identified the appellant when he was produced through video conferencing.
There is no explanation for not conducting the test identification parade at the stage of the investigation.
Avinash Vijay Kharat vs State Of Mah. Thr. Pso Ps Imamwada Nagpur ...
The investigation conducted in the 17 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt crime is conspicuously silent about all these aspects.
The appellant, as can be seen from the record, was not known to the victim prior to the alleged incident.
The appellant,
therefore, could not be the boyfriend of the victim.
The victim did not disclose the name of the boyfriend, who had sexual intercourse with her at that time.
In the facts and circumstances, I am of the opinion that the conviction and sentence on the basis of such tainted evidence cannot be sustained.
The doubtful circumstances highlighted hereinabove, would be sufficient to create a serious doubt about the involvement of the appellant in this crime.
15. Though, there is a statutory presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act with respect to the guilt of an accused, this presumption will not operate when the prosecution has failed to prove some foundational facts with respect to the case.
The presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act is not an absolute presumption.
It is a rebuttable presumption.
The presumption gets triggered only when the foundational facts are established by the prosecution beyond reasonable doubt.
The evidence on record must be sufficient to believe 18 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt the case of the prosecution and thereby support the very foundation of the case of the prosecution.
In this case, the very foundation of the case of the prosecution viz-a-viz the charge against the accused has been shaken.
In my view, therefore, the presumption under Section 29 of the POCSO Act would not get automatically attracted/triggered.
16. There are numerous lacunae in the case.
The prosecution has failed to connect all the dots by leading cogent and concrete evidence.
The evidence of the victim is not sufficient to prove the complicity of the appellant in the commission of the alleged offence.
As such, the appellant deserves benefit of doubt.
opennyai_summary.decision:
The appeal, therefore, deserves to be allowed.
17. The Criminal Appeal is allowed.
(i) The judgment and order of conviction and sentence, passed against the appellant by learned District and Sessions Judge-11, Nagpur, dated 13.01.2022 in Special Child Case No. 160/2019, is quashed and set aside.
on 9 October, 2024
(ii) Appellant - Avinash Vijay Kharat is acquitted of the offences punishable under Section 376(2)(n), 323 of the Indian Penal 19 APPEAL287.22 (J).odt Code and under Section 6 of the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012.
(iii) The appellant is in jail.
He be released forthwith, if not required in any other crime/case.
18. Ms. Radha Mishra, learned advocate appointed to represent respondent no.2/victim is entitled to get her fees.
The High Court Legal Services Sub Committee, Nagpur is directed to pay the fees to the learned appointed advocate, as per the Rules.
19 . The appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
